fullText:
Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X

Elon Musk has issued an angry tirade at the film-maker behind a four-hour documentary about his life and influence, labelling the director Alex Gibney a “bitter old man” who has “zero integrity”.

Gibney, who has previously made films about the collapse of Enron, WikiLeaks and Vladimir Putin, premiered his Musk documentary at the Venice film festival this week. He said he believed the world’s richest man was “extremely dangerous”.

In a series of posts on X, which Musk bought for $44bn in 2022, the tech mogul railed against the film as a “hit piece that misses”, adding its four-hour length also made the documentary, which is highly critical of Musk, “as boring af”.

Musk also appeared to push at conspiracy theory, reposting an image depicting the Democratic party as a puppet, controlling another puppet labelled “Team Soros” – a reference to the billionaire George Soros, who has supported progressive causes.

That puppet in turn controls another labelled “Alex Gibney”, while the Gibney puppet controls another labelled “Hollywood”. In response to the picture, Musk stated: “Accurate.”

In response to a supporter who said he had never heard of Gibney until his Musk film, Musk replied: “It’s a psy op” – a reference to a planned “psychological operation” designed to influence the public’s thoughts.

“Gibney has zero integrity. Zero,” said Musk. “Fortunately, his movies are boring af … It’s a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours.

“Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind) … He’s a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago.

“Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”

The documentary has caused stirs since its premier, as have the claims made by some of those involved in the film.

Musk specifically denied a claim made by his ex-partner, the former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair, that his team offered her $40m to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their time together. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” he wrote.

Musk also amplified a post by the podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of Donald Trump’s powerful adviser Stephen Miller and former communications director for Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. Miller complained about the alleged absence of Musk acquaintances and allies in the film.

“It simply can’t be ‘definitive’ if the people who were present didn’t participate,” she said. “This fictional movie is a hit job by a self-obsessed Hollywood director.”

Musk’s influence on public discourse through X, and the content it prioritises, is having international ripples. While he has repeatedly intervened in the immigration debate in the UK, he also celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland in this week’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking at a press conference in Venice, Gibney said he had encountered a “sense of fear” among people he approached over his film. He surmised that Musk’s childhood in South Africa may account for how he behaves now.

“He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”

fullText:
Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
In August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an ancient video of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.

Since then, plenty of companies have tried to be the first to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.

Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?

Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it was introducing time limits for game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right: that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?

In the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.

This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of a lot of data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.

The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are now more expensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spending went on data centres and AI infrastructure in the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.

Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in a blog post announcing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?

Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has been riding high on the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.

I have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived into Kingdom Come Deliverance II – think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.

I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.

I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to at least get to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.

Available on: Xbox, PlayStation 5, PC

 Estimated playtime: 55+ hours

A Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcoming Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out the demo here.

For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has written this excellent long-read on Japanese publisher Capcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.

Patrick Miller – better known as pattheflip – has published a thought-provoking reflection on how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”

At the end of last week, the White House released this horrible little propaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular game was later removed after The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.

Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar

‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world

Reader Piero sent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):

“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such as Kingdom Come Deliverance, Skyrim and the Baldur’s Gate series, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”

You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of course Disco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; like Citizen Sleeper, it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things about Eastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggest Pentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. And Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles is worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.

title: Colorado football receives AP Top 25 votes after Georgia Tech win
description: Colorado received votes in the AP Top 25 for the first time since 2025 after beating Georgia Tech, while four Big 12 teams remain ranked.
fullText:
Colorado appeared on the AP Top 25 Poll for the first time since 2025, not as a ranked team but as a team that received a few votes. This follows a thrilling 14-13 win over Georgia Tech in the season opener, in which they had a much-improved run defense and a formidable rushing attack.

Four Big 12 teams are ranked, the same as last week. Texas Tech remains the top-ranked team in the Big 12 but dropped from No. 12 to No. 13. BYU also dropped a spot despite a dominant win in their season opener. Utah and Houston moved up in the polls after their victories.

In addition to the Buffaloes, two other Big 12 teams received votes. Arizona received 33 votes after their victory over Northern Arizona, while ASU had two votes after defeating Morgan State 70-7.

Elsewhere in college football, Louisville and Virginia are in the top 25 after not being ranked going into the season. The Cardinals are the only team currently ranked with a loss after nearly defeating Ole Miss in their opener. The biggest jump among teams ranked in the initial poll is LSU, which moved from No. 11 to No. 8 after a 51-10 win over Clemson.

Michigan, which started the season ranked No. 16 in the country, is no longer ranked despite its controversial win against Western Michigan. Another notable drop is Oregon. After nearly getting beaten by Boise State, who received 86 votes in the poll, the Ducks dropped from No. 2 to No. 6. Texas A&M and Washington both dropped two spots.

Colorado hopes to continue its upward trend in the poll with a Week 2 matchup against a manageable Weber State team where the Buffs are heavily favored.

fullText:
Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says

Datacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research.

Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK.

Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation.

Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons.

It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections.

Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt.

Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them.

James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds.

“Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.”

To underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility.

The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.”

Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity.

Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet.

Narayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.”

Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are.

‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.”

In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”.

A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”

description: Meta Platforms Inc. has run more than 300 advertisements on Instagram and Facebook containing suspected child sexual abuse material this year, according to a report Tuesday by the nonprofit Tech Transparency Project.
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. has run more than 300 advertisements on Instagram and Facebook containing suspected child sexual abuse material this year, according to a report Tuesday by the nonprofit Tech Transparency Project.

The ads collectively reached more than 29,000 people and typically used artificial intelligence to depict young children being molested, TTP said. Many served to promote deepfake "nudify" apps, which were the subject of an earlier report by the group, which tracked their source to app developers and a Meta advertising partner in China. TTP is a research arm of the Washington, DC-based nonpartisan corporate and government watchdog Campaign for Accountability.

The failure to prevent such material appearing on Meta's services, used by billions globally, comes as the company faces unprecedented scrutiny for social media's alleged harms to children. The ads violate Meta's own policies prohibiting child exploitation, abuse and nudity, along with US federal laws. TTP said it reported the ads to the Congressionally mandated National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

"Content involving child sexual abuse is among the most serious that can be found online," said Katie Paul, TTP's director. "But this content isn't hiding in dark corners of the internet. It's being used in paid ads on Meta platforms."

In one instance, TTP said it found ads that used a photo a young girl had posted to her Instagram account in which she was wearing a sports uniform. The ad animated her image into a video in which she is depicted performing a sex act, TTP said. Another ad showed a preteen girl removing her shirt, with accompanying text promising "dark" content.

"We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated," Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Bloomberg News. Many of the ads flagged had already been removed, he said. Those behind such activity frequently shift tactics to circumvent Meta's systems, and the company continues to strengthen its detection and enforcement, he added.

TTP in July reported Meta had shown thousands of sexually suggestive ads for nudification apps, which are designed to digitally remove clothing or place photos of real people into graphic images of videos. The new findings pertain to ads that are more graphic, TTP says.

Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday.

Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras.

OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July.

OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.

But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment.

OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks.

The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.)

OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks.

As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market.

Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal

New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school

Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’

Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI

Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images

The US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation.

Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month.

Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram.

Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners.

In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat.

London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.

Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history.

In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun.

title: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film

fullText:
Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

title: I grew my salary to $112K after a career pivot. A layoff broke my heart and changed my perception of money and success.
description: A 32-year-old in Canada shares her salary journey from working in nutrition to making $112,000 in tech, and how a layoff changed her perspective.
fullText:
Evelyn Irwanto is a 32-year-old living in Toronto. She was a senior manager at a marketing and branding consultancy, making CA$155,000, or roughly $112,000, before she was laid off in September 2025. Business Insider has verified Irwanto's income and employment history with documentation. The following as-told-to essay has been edited for length and clarity.

I got into health and fitness near the end of high school and thought I wanted to be a dietitian. Deep down, though, I truly had no idea what I wanted to do.

I grew up in a pretty typical Asian immigrant family. My parents were pushing me toward more traditional fields like business, medicine, or law. In hindsight, a nutrition career was maybe a little act of rebellion — I wanted to do something that they didn't approve of.

I was pretty steadfast, so they let me go for it, but I probably should've listened to them.

Spoiler alert: I didn't go into a career in dietetics. Here's my salary journey.

After graduating with a degree in nutrition and food in 2017, I got a part-time role as a nutrition associate, making around $14 Canadian dollars an hour. I also worked as a server on the side, for around CA$11 an hour plus tips.

It was tough, but at that time, I was young and had energy. I'd moved out on my own, and the jobs worked with my schedule.

The nutrition associate job was typically 8-to-4 shifts, and then I'd do double shifts and serve at night, starting from 5 p.m. It was fun. I really enjoyed serving.

I did that for 10 months, from August 2017 through May 2018.

Salary Journeys is Business Insider's first-person series following real people and their real paychecks — how they built their income, what it means for their lives, and what they learned along the way. If you're willing to share how your salary has changed over time, please fill out this Google Form.

During that time, I was looking for a full-time position, but after not being able to find one, I started to realize I didn't want to do nutrition full-time.

I'd already kind of known it in college, around the time I took a gap year off school after going to Melbourne for an exchange program, but I kept following through the motions.

In mid-2018, I left my nutrition associate and serving jobs, subleased my apartment, and took some time off to travel. I call it my "Eat, Pray, Love" moment because I bought a one-way ticket to South America and backpacked for about four months to figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

It gave me clarity and the courage to accept what I knew deep down already: I don't know what I want to do; I just know I don't want to do this. And I owe it to myself to try to pivot.

Once I got back, I put applications out to all kinds of jobs that seemed remotely interesting.

Through a local Facebook group, I found a seasonal, contract role as a customer service and community management coordinator with a small marketing agency that paid CA$15 an hour.

I got the job in October 2018. It was only a seasonal role, my commute was an hour and a half, and I made less than I'd been making previously, but I was still ecstatic because it was my first foot out the door of nutrition, and I got to learn and try something new.

My next role was as a contractor for a Big Tech software company as a credit and collections analyst. A friend working in that position at the time reached out about their team looking for more people. I had no idea what credit and collections was, but it seemed like a great opportunity to get into a Big Tech, Fortune 500 company.

It also came with higher pay — CA$22 an hour — and the potential to go full-time.

It was a big adjustment, but it was exciting. I was like, Oh my gosh! You get to dress up in corporate clothing, learn so much about processes and policies, and be part of a team. There were very clear metrics and KPIs, which I'd never had before. It was a learning experience.

My parents were super happy. They worried at first because I'd spent so much time doing a nutrition degree, but once I started getting opportunities like at this Big Tech company, they were like, "OK, it seems like this is working out for you."

My manager at the time recommended I move to a different team under the credit and collections department because there were more opportunities to get converted, so I did.

I ended up getting converted full-time in late 2019, and my pay was CA$25.88 an hour, with eligibility for a CA$2,700 bonus annually.

I worked really hard on that team for about a year and eight months — almost like I had to prove myself even more than other people because I didn't have the backing of a relevant degree.

But I knew I didn't want to stay in credit and collections forever; I enjoyed it and was good at it, but long-term, the day-to-day job and income potential didn't match up to what I wanted. From the very beginning, I was like, "I want to climb the corporate ladder."

A supervisor position opened up, which I applied for. At that time, it was two levels higher than me, which was tough to justify to HR and the people team, but I applied and worked really hard on the case study. The managers and the panel interview knew me as a hard worker, and I ended up getting that position.

That year — 2021 — I made around CA$81,000. My parents were super proud when I got promoted.

I learned a lot from that supervisor role, but it didn't take me very long to start applying for other jobs within the company in order to fulfill my ultimate goal of leaving collections.

In December 2021, I ended up getting a sales operations business process specialist role within the company's revenue operations department. My salary was around CA$91,700.

A lot of the job was identifying gaps within processes and policies, talking to stakeholders, and aligning teams, which was the stuff that I liked to do. I stayed there for just over a year. I enjoyed the job, but also felt isolated because of COVID and remote work.

It was also less busy, and I'm someone who can't sit still and needs to be doing a lot. It made me wonder, am I providing value or impact? I'd have conversations with my skip-level manager, asking about growth opportunities. I also started to feel the red tape a lot with getting ideas approved, which made me a little disgruntled.

A lot of my friends were working in startups at that time. I also had a mentor within the company who recommended, based on my goals, that I look into startups. I started applying.

One of my friends posted a LinkedIn opportunity for a revenue operations manager at a Series A tech company based in Toronto. I ended up getting a referral and got the job.

The pay was CA$100,000 plus equity, which felt mind-blowing. I was proud and knew I was qualified, but I still felt some imposter syndrome.

Joining the startup slapped me across the face; it was a big learning curve. But that was also kind of what I wanted. You're doing it all — wearing different hats, with no guidelines or scope — and no one's

telling you what to do. You just do what needs to be done and figure it out.

It was probably one of my favorite roles to date. I met friends that I'm still friends with, and had good management that really supported me and wanted me to grow. I learned so much in that role, which is why I ended up staying there for almost two years. I got a raise to CA$103,000, and then to CA$108,000, or around $78,000.

I ended up leaving because I was really gunning for a promotion in my role as revenue operations manager, and it felt like it was dangled but never happened.

I was frustrated and ended up getting recruited by the next company, a marketing and branding consultancy.

They offered me CA$150,000, which I negotiated up to CA$155,000, and a title boost to senior manager instead of manager. The opportunity felt too good to be true and seemed like it fit my experience. It would've been silly for me not to take it, so I did.

Coming into the role was a pretty big change. I went through months of burnout, not feeling really supported, and having an existential crisis about what I was doing with my life.

I thought, I can't leave this job because I've only been here for X months. I don't want to be seen as a job-hopper. It was tough.

I ended up taking a leave of absence, during which time I did a lot of therapy. I really felt ready to come back with a new attitude and perspective on things like balance.

But in September 2025, the Friday before I was supposed to come back, I was laid off. The formal reason they gave was due to a restructuring.

I cried; it was heartbreaking and jarring.

When I think back to that day, it's still very emotional. I think it ended up working out for the best, but it was tough. It felt like a gut punch.

I'd already started applying to jobs during my mental health leave to see what other options were out there. Once I got laid off, I started really pouring myself into interviews.

I was interested in freelancing, so I started talking to people about what that looked like. I ended up getting introduced to the owner of a revenue operations consultancy here in Toronto. I met him for coffee, and we really hit it off. He told me that he couldn't guarantee me a set amount of hours, but at the time, he had 10 hours for the month ahead.

That was the same time that I got two different offers, both with salaries in the mid-six-figures, but the thought of going back to corporate made me feel so depleted, so I turned them down.

Thanks to my severance package, I had a bit of runway to explore doing my own thing. I ended up taking the consultancy to just try it out, and started content creation.

In June, I actually surpassed my monthly corporate salary. I feel like I was able to prove that I could do it and have full confidence that I can continue. I feel like there are so many possibilities.

I have a different perspective on money now; it's not the most important thing for me, and even if I'm not able to hit my goal of replacing my tech salary for whatever reason, I'll be okay with it because I genuinely love everything that I'm doing right now. I feel like I have this new sense of control that I didn't have in the corporate world.

I just feel like there are so many possibilities out there that this is only the beginning. In corporate, it felt like there was kind of a ceiling to how far I could go, and to move up, I'd have to give up so much; I hear about all these VPs and C-suite level executives who don't even see their kids.

With this new kind of portfolio career consisting of content creation and freelancing, I have so much more autonomy in what I get to do. I get to choose the opportunities that fulfill me, while still not dimming my income potential.

I still struggle with having a scarcity mindset of always feeling like I have to prove myself and not having enough. Maybe it's because my family wasn't rich, so that was something that I had to fulfill for myself and for them, to show everybody that I could do it.

It's almost like money, titles, and salary were the epitome of success to me. Now I realize that there's so much more than that.

fullText:
Matt Clifford forced to stand down amid disquiet from senior MPs over his new full-time job at AI company

The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit has been forced to stand down after taking a job with the San Francisco AI firm Anthropic, in a move senior MPs called a “clear conflict of interest”.

Matt Clifford announced last week that he was taking a full-time job working for the company behind the Claude chatbot, “leading its engagement” with governments outside the US – including the UK. But he retained his leadership at the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria), which funds frontier science and tech projects.

The move sparked concern, with Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the Commons science, innovation and technology committee, calling it a “clear conflict of interest” and outlining her disquiet in a letter to the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.

At the time Clifford’s new employer said he would recuse himself from any Anthropic-related business at Aria in an arrangement that had been agreed with the government.

Clifford announced on Monday: “I have decided to step down to ensure my new role at Anthropic doesn’t become a distraction from Aria’s incredible work.” He said he would stay in place until 6 November “with appropriate safeguards against potential conflicts in place”.

Onwurah welcomed the move but said questions remained, including “how this situation arose, what conflict of interest assessments were undertaken and what safeguards are in place to protect confidence in Aria’s governance.”

Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of government AI policy, welcomed Clifford’s resignation. “If we are to rebuild trust in the government, we need to see a clear line between tech interests and those of citizens and the nation,” she said.

Clifford’s full-time Anthropic role highlighted a revolving door between the government and AI companies. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak has taken jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft, and the former chancellor George Osborne works for OpenAI. They followed Nick Clegg, who held a senior role with Meta until 2025.

Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, had said taking extensive knowledge about a policy as sensitive as AI to a private sector company shortly after leaving government could weaken the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.

On Monday the risks of the race to ever more powerful AIs were again highlighted by the AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, who gave a statement supporting a private member’s bill being introduced on Tuesday in the UK parliament to prohibit the creation of artificial superintelligence, warning: “Losing control over AI smarter than ourselves … could even lead to human extinction.”

Clifford was appointed Keir Starmer’s AI adviser in January 2025 but stepped down for personal reasons after six months in the role.

The 40-year-old made his career in the private sector as the co-founder of the venture capital outfit Entrepreneurs First, becoming a pivotal figure in the UK tech scene. As well taking the chair of Aria in 2022, he became a key adviser to Sunak and played a prominent role in organising the 2023 AI safety summit in the UK. He also helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.

title: This company says it can help cool the planet for $10 billion a year; scientists are raising red flags
description: Stardust Solutions is developing a particle to spray into the atmosphere and dim the sun. Scientists are worried the technology could have huge global consequences.
fullText:
One company has a simple-sounding plan to help save the planet: take a food additive and the mineral that makes eggshells hard, produce tiny particles out of them, spray them into the atmosphere and cool the world.

Stardust Solutions, an Israeli-US company founded in 2023 and led by two former Israeli government nuclear physicists, is pushing ahead in the race to develop solar geoengineering, a controversial technology aimed at artificially bringing down global temperatures by dimming the sun.

There are many different solar geoengineering methods, but perhaps the most researched — and the one Stardust focuses on — involves spraying tiny particles into the stratosphere from high-altitude aircraft or balloons to reflect the sun's energy away from Earth and back into space.

It's an artificial version of a natural phenomenon. Volcanic eruptions sometimes spew so much sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere it can temporarily lower global temperatures. In 1991, the eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines injected enough into the atmosphere to produce cooling of 0.9 degrees Fahrenheit (0.5 Celsius) for more than a year.

As humans burn fossil fuels and heat the planet, the question of whether solar geoengineering can and should move from theory to reality is gaining prominence.

⛈️ Get your local forecast with the CNN Weather app

The technology is a "critical tool" for governments to consider as the global thermostat runs terrifyingly hot, said Stardust's CEO Yanai Yedvab, although he stressed it's neither a silver bullet for climate change nor a substitute for addressing its root causes.

Many scientists, however, have expressed fears that solar geoengineering could have disastrous global implications, including dramatically altering weather patterns. And some experts are raising red flags that a for-profit company is developing proprietary technology that could have huge and unpredictable repercussions.

"When the whole world is at stake, satisfying the needs of venture capitalists for profits should not enter at all into decisions about what, if anything, should be deployed," said Raymond Pierrehumbert, professor of planetary physics at the University of Oxford.

Scientists have been researching solar geoengineering for decades, but private companies are starting to pop up. Of these, Stardust is arguably the most high profile, not least because it's the best funded, having raised $75 million from investors.

The company was formed in the wake of the pandemic. Yedvab and his co-founder, Amyad Spector, landed on solar geoengineering as they explored ways to help address the climate crisis.

When it comes to spraying particles in the atmosphere, most solar geoengineering research and development focuses on sulfur dioxide, mimicking volcanic eruptions. But sulfur dioxide can have negative impacts, including contributing to acid rain and ozone layer depletion.

Stardust wanted to develop a material "that will be better, will be safer, that could be controlled," Yedvab said. Earlier this year, it revealed its particle designs in a series of scientific papers, which await peer review.

The company has produced two particles: One from amorphous silica, commonly used as an anti-caking additive in foods, toothpaste and cosmetics; the other is made from a core of calcium carbonate, the main component in eggshells, surrounded by a shell of amorphous silica.

Both compounds occur naturally, but can be created synthetically. And these are commonly used substances, Yedvab said. Amorphous silica, for example, was released into the New York City subway in 2016, as part of a Department of Homeland Security test designed to simulate the impacts of a potential biological attack. It's an anecdote that helps highlight how safe silica is considered to be, Yedvab said.

Every million tons of particles would lead to 0.9 degrees Fahrenheit of cooling, and would need be replenished every year, Yedvab said. Each million-ton deployment would cost roughly $10 billion. It's a lot, he acknowledged, but still a small fraction of the damage climate change-related disasters are already causing.

But experts have raised concerns. In addition to being queasy about private business attempting to alter the climate, some are also concerned about the impacts on global climate and weather, as well as human health.

David Keith, a professor of geophysical sciences at the University of Chicago who is best known for his research on solar geoengineering, said Stardust is "greatly overclaiming to say that they're confident the risks [of their particles] are lower than with sulfur." One concern is the "hitchhiker hypothesis" — that particles in the air can pick up metals or other substances that can cause harm when people breathe them in.

Stardust said its particle design takes these risks into account, but whether they will work at scale and how they might behave in the atmosphere is unclear, said Kelly Wanser, executive director of SilverLining, a nonprofit climate research organization.

"Solar geoengineering engages some of the least understood aspects of the climate system," said Pierrehumbert, adding that no small-scale experiment can indicate how Earth systems would respond to a full-scale deployment.

So far, the company has limited its tests to the lab. Launching outdoor tests is the next step, but history suggests this will be fraught. Plans by Harvard scientists to conduct test flights for solar geoengineering in Arctic Sweden were abandoned in 2021 after intense local opposition. A rogue experiment by US startup Make Sunsets in Mexico in 2022 led the country to ban solar geoengineering experiments.

Stardust, which hopes to start outdoor tests in the next few years, would only run them "under supervision and direct guidance of governments," Yedvab said. He compared the process to testing life-saving drugs. They would start with very small-scale tests, with clearly defined success criteria, before graduating to larger-scale tests.

The company says it's already engaging policymakers to try to build a regulatory framework around testing. Decisions on whether the tech is ever deployed belong "solely in governments," Yedvab said.

Still, Stardust is a for-profit company with a financial incentive in the deployment of this technology, some experts say, and that has raised alarms. "Proprietary technology and profit motives are directly at odds with the transparency needed to legitimize [solar geoengineering] research," Keith wrote in a blogpost last year.

Sarah Doherty, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at the University of Washington, who leads a solar geoengineering research team, said "the current science does not support making financial bets on, or driving society toward, specific approaches."

Yedvab said most groundbreaking technologies benefitting humanity have been made by for-profit companies, albeit often building on academic research.

But the stakes are achingly high. Solar geoengineering could open the door to a host of unintended consequences, including the potential to alter rainfall patterns and shift monsoons, which could have big repercussions for food production, scientists say.

Perhaps most alarming is the prospect of "termination shock." This is the idea that, once started, solar geoengineering would have to be maintained indefinitely. If stopped suddenly, "the world is then faced with a catastrophic, sudden warming playing out over just a few years," Pierrehumbert said.

Stardust says its technology can be tuned up or down, meaning deployment can be scaled down gradually. The particles fall out of the atmosphere after roughly a year "so the level of cooling remains a continuing, adjustable choice in the hands of governments and termination shock can be avoided," Yedvab said.

Some remain unconvinced. Deploying the technology would bring "profound systemic uncertainty" and the "potential to destabilize the global climate system further," a recent study concluded.

Thorny ethical issues also abound, including who gets to choose when and how solar geoengineering is deployed, who pays for it and what happens if some countries benefit while others are harmed.

"I worry that decisions about if, when, and how to deploy solar engineering will not be made by poor countries but rather by rich countries and private investors," said Chukwumerije Okereke, professor in global governance and public policy at the University of Bristol.

Then there's the fear this technology will be seized on as a reason not to make deep cuts to planet-heating pollution, which means significantly reducing the amount of fossil fuels we burn.

This is a "valid concern," said Yedvab, but it should be balanced with what he called "moral imperatives." Stardust's argument is that as the impacts of climate change get increasingly severe and deadly, governments must have options.

Solar geoengineering could "buy humanity the decades needed" to address the underlying causes of climate change, Yedvab said. "I believe the real risk is that a decade from now governments will face a decision on whether they need to deploy this option without having properly studied it and having safe options in front of them."

title: I took a 6-figure job at Amazon after stepping away from full-time entrepreneurship. A chance meeting led me back to my business.
description: Seun Phillips returned to his business, Stemnetics, after a one-year stint at Amazon. He used his tech experience to expand STEM education programs.
fullText:
Seun Phillips took a six-figure job at Amazon after stepping back from entrepreneurship.

A chance meeting with a principal prompted Phillips to return to his business, Stemnetics, full time.

He says Amazon's customer obsession and frugality still guide his work.

This as-told-to essay is based on an interview with Seun Phillips, the 42-year-old founder of Stemnetics, who is based in Los Angeles. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I was always interested in technology. My family got our first computer when I was in the third grade, and my four brothers and I would always game together. I was good at math and science, and my father said I should think about becoming an engineer.

In 2006, I graduated from the University of Michigan with a degree in electrical engineering. We had a career fair on campus. I remember my next class was about to start, but I saw Motorola. I decided to drop just one more résumé. They called me, and I got through the interview process. I became an electrical engineer focused on accessory compatibility for Motorola in Illinois.

I went on to become an entrepreneur, with a stint at Amazon in between, where I learned lessons I still use in my business today.

I launched Project Syncere in Chicago in March 2009. Its mission is to create pathways for underrepresented students to pursue careers in STEM. This was my first experience running a business, apart from selling CDs in high school. I'm still on the board.

I met my wife and moved to Detroit to be with her. We weren't looking to expand Project Syncere to another state, so in January 2014, I launched Stemnetics in Michigan, which runs hands-on STEM programs for kids.

I got a job as the vice president of education and engagement at the Michigan Science Center. I took the job because I had my first child and needed more financial stability.

I hired a full-time teacher and a part-time teacher through Indeed and Craigslist, so they kept the program running while I used my science center earnings to bootstrap the company. I wanted to keep Stemnetics running because I saw the potential.

I started searching for new roles, and a former colleague told me he was hiring at Amazon Robotics. The role involved identifying companies and startups developing technologies that could improve fulfillment, logistics, and supply chain operations. I understood the startup ecosystem, and I like bringing people together. I was interested.

I had six back-to-back interviews over Zoom, each centered on a different Amazon leadership principle. The ones that stayed with me were customer obsession, frugality, ownership, and bias for action. I still use them at Stemnetics: stay focused on who you serve, move quickly, and find a resourceful way forward without compromising quality.

I remember starting the interview process at 6 a.m. because I'm on Pacific Time. The last interview was with the person who ended up being my manager. I was hired with a six-figure salary.

My role focused on building partnerships with companies and startups.

I worked remotely, but I visited the office and a fulfillment center many times. The Amazon environment was very different from other Big Tech offices I heard about: There were standard cubicles and labs where you could see the technology being tested.

I wanted to see the robots in action at a fulfillment center so I could understand how everything moved. I'm very big on the why. I'm seeking partnerships, but why is it important? It was nice to see.

One thing I found really useful at Amazon was working backward. You start by writing a future press release describing the customer benefit you hope to create. It gives you a North Star for what you're building.

Another cool concept at Amazon was a Wellness Day. You're not supposed to use that as a vacation day — you're supposed to use it for professional development, catching up, anything that would support your mental health. My manager's manager made sure no meetings were scheduled, so it was truly all about wellness.

After about a year at Amazon, I was watching football at a sports bar when I started talking to a school principal. He told me he was trying to build a STEM lab. I told him I ran STEM programs, and we decided to meet.

I demonstrated the program at his school. Then the district heard about it. That was the moment I realized Stemnetics was ready for my full attention.

I was very close with my manager at Amazon, and there were opportunities there, but I think it was more about me betting on myself.

I used some of the Michigan curriculum to expand in California, and I'd pack the containers with teaching materials I'd bought on Amazon until the wee hours of the morning. My wife would come down, and our whole living room would be full of teaching materials, and then I'd drop the boxes off at different schools. I'd also teach the students and train the other instructors.

Today, we have an office with storage facilities for teaching materials and program managers who help with the training process. I've surpassed my Amazon earnings, we have over 35 employees, and we have over 30 programs running in Michigan and California. The impact we're making is very gratifying.

My favorite part of my job is visiting the classroom and seeing students screaming with excitement. We're really focused on sparking kids' interest and finding ways to help them become great problem solvers, think critically, be resilient, and be confident.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: ‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health minister

fullText:
James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs

Concern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects.

James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.

The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes.

Frith’s comment, in a letter to Layla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out.

Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money.

Palantir and its supporters say its AI-driven technology has cut NHS waiting lists for surgery. A spokesperson for the company said it was “helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 110,000 additional operations, a 15% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 6.8% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days”.

NHS England has reported similar numbers but said it could not “draw conclusions about cause and effect”. The government’s statistics watchdog is investigating the data.

Frith told Moran there had been an increase in NHS data opt-outs, in line with media interest in Palantir’s position.

Palantir’s government contracts have been beset by controversy. Ministers apologised after it emerged that the company’s staff had access to identifiable patient data.

London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has also blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding Palantir a £50m contract to use its AI to support investigations. He said Londoners wanted to see public money paid only to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir is suing over the mayor’s decision.

Frith said the rise in opt-outs was “modest” but would still be monitored. Opting out does not stop an individual’s records from being used for direct care, such as live operations. However, it prevents it being used for research and planning.

Frith said: “It may not be possible to realise the benefits of the 10-year health plan if patients stop sharing their data.”

Foxglove, a tech equity campaign, welcomed the minister’s acknowledgment of apparent public mistrust of Palantir. “Doctors and patients have been warning about the threat this poses to NHS care, and tens of thousands of people have opted out in just the last few months,” said Tom Hegarty, its head of communications.

“People are right to be concerned given … its founder, Trump ally Peter Thiel, going on record to opine that the NHS makes people sick.”

Frith indicated a policy shift on whether the Palantir-powered platform must be used by NHS trusts. In July, a health minister told parliament that health trusts would be told they “must use” parts of NHS England’s federated platform, which is controlled using Palantir technology. Now Frith has said “there is no requirement to use the FDP” and they may “prefer an alternative”.

Moran, who is a Liberal Democrat MP, said she welcomed the “softened stance” on whether adoption of the FDP was mandatory but added: “We remain of the view that the government should switch provider and not extend the current contract. Given how long this process could take, ministers need to act decisively and quickly, and not put this decision off until February.”

title: Designers should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders say
description:
Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff
Professional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector.
With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them.
